messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Electrician
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 78

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Time of Day: The same time of day the event occurred, Dissociative Feeling: Beginning to feel detached or unreal, Auditory (Door): Doors opening or slamming
  Maladaptive Strategies: Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking, Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
  Threat: Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
  Memory: Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
  Negative Appraisals: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, Hopelessness: I have no future, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kai is a 42-year-old electrician of Oceania descent who lives with his partner in a quiet suburban neighborhood. He came to therapy at his partner’s urging, after months of what he describes as “falling apart” following a brutal assault in the parking lot of a job site six months ago. The attack happened at dusk, around 6:15 PM, as he was packing his tools into his van. Two men cornered him, demanding his wallet and phone. When he hesitated, one slammed a heavy metal door from a nearby dumpster against his back, while the other punched him in the ribs. The memory that haunts him most is not the full sequence but isolated, vivid snapshots: the sound of the door slamming, the dull thud against his spine, the feeling of his knees buckling onto asphalt. He recalls these moments as frozen pictures, each one distinct and incomplete, as if his mind has edited out the rest. What remains is a fragmentary loop of guilt—he cannot shake the belief that he should have fought back, should have seen it coming, and that the attack happened because of the sort of person he is: someone too trusting, too slow, too weak.

In the weeks that followed, Kai began to notice that the time of day—late afternoon, the light beginning to fade—would trigger a sudden, visceral shift. As the clock edged toward 6 PM, his chest would tighten and his surroundings would feel unreal, as if he were watching himself from a distance. That same dissociative feeling, coupled with the sound of a door opening or slamming at work or at home, would send him straight into a state of hypervigilance. A colleague shutting a cabinet too hard would make him flinch, and he would catch himself scanning the parking lot for escape routes. These triggers also pulled him back into the fragmented memories: the slamming door, the guilt, the incomplete picture of what exactly happened. And each time, the thought would surface again: *This happened because of who I am.* Kai had come to believe that his character was fundamentally flawed, that another man would have handled the situation differently, and that his future was effectively over.

To manage the constant dread, Kai developed a set of habits that seemed to help in the moment but only deepened his isolation. After work, he would retreat to the basement and spend hours scrolling through his phone, playing games, or drinking beer until he felt numb. He avoided any television show or film that involved violence or confrontation, because even fictional depictions would bring the memory roaring back. These strategies worked briefly, but they also reinforced his sense of hopelessness—each evening spent escaping reminded him that he was not getting better, that he was stuck. His partner noticed he was drinking more and withdrawing from their shared routines, and they argued about it, which only made Kai feel more convinced that he was a burden.

The threat system Kai now lives with is relentless. He startles violently at unexpected movement—someone stepping into his peripheral vision at a hardware store will make him drop his keys. He reacts with alarm when his partner touches him from behind, even gently. He has begun avoiding unfamiliar places altogether, because he cannot assess the danger in advance. He sticks to the same grocery store, the same route home, the same few job sites he knows. This avoidance has cost him work; he turned down a lucrative contract that required traveling to a new part of the city. The threat is not just external—it feeds into his memory, because every startle reminds him of the assault, and every reminder reinforces his belief that he is broken. And the triggers themselves seem to multiply: now, even the sound of a car door at dusk can set him off, and he finds himself scanning for danger in his own backyard.

What finally brought Kai to seek help was a moment of clarity. Last week, his partner came home unexpectedly and found him sitting in the dark basement at 6:15 PM, phone in hand, a half-empty bottle of whiskey on the floor, staring at the wall. He had been there for three hours. When she asked what was wrong, he could only say, “I don’t know how to stop this.” He is terrified that he will never feel safe again, that the assault has permanently reshaped who he is, and that his relationship will not survive his retreat into avoidance. But beneath that fear, there is a fragile hope: that if he can understand why his mind keeps pulling him back to those frozen moments, he might finally find a way out.
